connection: Session 13 established the prerequisite model. This session applies it to capability constraints with observable TimeLedger examples.
objectives: Explain constraints state which operations generic code may safely perform without runtime guessing.
Predict behavior before running a focused capability constraints example.
Apply generic constraints without weakening existing domain invariants.
Verify the behavior with automated tests.

visuals.explanation: Start by identifying the values, identities, and capabilities involved in capability constraints.

options: To make the mental model testable

concept.title: Build the behavioral model
paragraphs: The central rule is that constraints state which operations generic code may safely perform without runtime guessing.
Names and syntax matter because they communicate whether code copies, aliases, enumerates, compares, or constrains a value.
concept.code: static T Later<T>(T left, T right) where T : IComparable<T>

concept.title: Program to the required capability
paragraphs: A caller should not need to provide more capability than the operation consumes.
Concrete implementations remain useful at construction boundaries; interfaces and generic contracts keep consuming code focused.
concept.code:
// Prefer the smallest contract that supports the operation.
static T Later<T>(T left, T right) where T : IComparable<T>

concept.title: Verify cause and effect
paragraphs: The lab changes one behavior at a time and uses tests to preserve the observation.
If the prediction differs from the result, explain the language rule before continuing.

lab.objective: Add a focused TimeLedger example that demonstrates generic constraints.
lab.startingCondition: Sessions 01–13 are complete and the solution builds with all existing tests passing.
steps: Read the starting test and predict the result using the session mental model.
Add src/TimeLedger.Domain/GenericRules.cs with the smallest API needed for the example.
Add tests/TimeLedger.Domain.Tests/GenericRulesTests.cs to check the important before-and-after behavior.
Run the focused tests, then run the complete Release test suite.
Review whether each parameter and return type exposes only the capability it needs.
lab.expectedBehavior: The new tests demonstrate constraints state which operations generic code may safely perform without runtime guessing; all existing behavior remains green.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeLedger.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeLedger.sln --configuration Release

review: The example isolates one primary concept.
Public types express the minimum required capability.
Names describe behavior rather than implementation trivia.
Tests cover the important cause-and-effect relationship.
Nullable analysis remains enabled with no warnings.
The entire solution builds and all tests pass.

postQuiz.prompt: What did the lab establish about generic constraints?
options: constraints state which operations generic code may safely perform without runtime guessing
The compiler cannot describe the behavior
Tests replace the need for a mental model
postQuiz.explanation: The test makes the language rule observable and repeatable.

postQuiz.prompt: Why run the entire suite after the focused test?
options: To detect regressions across cumulative code
postQuiz.explanation: The course application grows cumulatively, so earlier guarantees must remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: When should a concrete collection or implementation leak into an API?
options: Only when its specific capability is part of the contract
postQuiz.explanation: Expose concrete capability only when callers genuinely need it.

reflections: How would you explain generic constraints without using a memory-location shortcut?
Which compiler error or test most clearly reveals the contract?
Where could an unnecessarily concrete type make future change harder?
whatBreaks: Removing the new domain example removes the executable model for capability constraints. Removing its tests allows subtle changes to assignment, equality, enumeration, or generic contracts to pass unnoticed. Widening the API unnecessarily gives callers capabilities the operation does not need.
summary: This session established that constraints state which operations generic code may safely perform without runtime guessing. The TimeLedger example, tests, and API review turn that rule into durable engineering practice.
